newsitem.title: USA: U.S. inmate to wed hours before execution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. inmate to wed hours before execution.

text.p: Convicted muderer Joseph O'Dell will marry on Wednesday then, barring an 11th-hour reprieve, die a few hours later.

O'Dell, whose cause has been celebrated in Italy and championed by Pope John Paul II, is due to be executed by lethal injection at 9 p.m. EDT (0100 GMT Thursday) for the 1985 rape and murder of Helen Schartner of Virginia Beach.
He will marry his volunteer paralegal Lori Urs between noon and 1 p.m. in the death house at the Greensville Correctional Centre, prison spokesman David Botkins said.
Warden David Garraghty had given the couple permission to wed, he said. Former death row chaplain Reverend Russell Ford will conduct the ceremony.
Virginia authorities say they intend to go ahead with the execution despite appeals for clemency from Pope John Paul and authorities in Italy, where O'Dell has found wide support.
Police said O'Dell, who was found guilty in 1985, said he abducted, pistol-whipped, raped and strangled the 44-year-old secretary before dumping her body in a field.
The Italian interest has bewildered and annoyed Schartner's family.
"We are all very fragile at this point," her sister Gail Lee told the Virginia Pilot newspaper. "Mama can't talk without crying. It's just like the Italians hate us."

"I used to have great respect for that country and its history and its art...now I never want to go there. I never want to set foot on their soil. Because by listening to just one side of this case, they in essence have said to my family. 'You are worthless. Helen's life didn't matter."
Just why Italy is so gripped by O'Dell, who has a long criminal record and has no ties to the country, is a mystery.

The Pope and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi have led a chorus of protest against his death sentence. Their appeals have encouraged street protests and vigils, particularly outside the U.S. embassy in Rome.
O'Dell has been made an honorary citizen of the city of Palermo and has said he wants to be buried there if his execution goes forward as planned.

Italy, which has no death penalty in civilian criminal cases, is among the most vocal supporters of a worldwide ban on capital punishment. It also refuses to extradite non-Italians from Italy to countries where they might face execution.
Gov. George Allen, a Republican known for his vigorous anti-crime stance, has said he believes O'Dell is guilty and refused to allow new DNA testing in the case.

The condemned man's supporters questioned the testing. A DNA test done on O'Dell's shirt in 1990 showed that blood on it did not belong to O'Dell or Schartner. But tests on the blood on his jacket showed by odds of 166,000 to one that the blood was Schartner's.
O'Dell's "spiritual adviser" is Sister Helen Prejean, author of "Dead Man Walking," the best-selling book that was made into a movie.
The execution was orginally scheduled for Dec. 18, 1996, but was stayed that day by the U.S. Supreme Court.
